transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Korva Coleman.
President Trump says Russia released detained American Stephen Hubbard.
Russia imprisoned the 74-year-old Hubbard for allegedly fighting for Ukraine.
News of his release comes as White House envoy Steve Whitcock visits Russia for talks with
President Vladimir Putin.
In fairs Charles Maine's reports from Moscow, they're talking about Russia's war in Ukraine.
Whitcock will join Putin for talks in St. Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital
and hometown of the Kremlin leader.
The trip comes just one day after Whitcock was in neighboring Norway for meetings with
Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky and European leaders that participants described
as constructive.
That in itself would seem an improvement to the past 10 days, during which President Trump
has repeatedly blamed Zelensky for being the primary obstacle to a peace deal and called
for new leadership in Kiev.
Trump has also lambasted Ukraine for responding to Kremlin attacks with drone strikes on Russia's
energy industry, a factor Trump claims is the key driver behind surging gas prices in
the U.S.
Charles Maine's NPR News, Moscow.
More than 80 volunteers from the Israel Organization, rabbis for human rights, and some American
activists have been detained by Israeli security forces.
They were helping Palestinians harvest olives from their grove, close to a settlement in
the occupied West Bank.
One of those detained is New York congressional candidate Brad Lander, and Piers Ruth Sherlock
was at the scene.
According to two Israeli lawyers we spoke with, it's the largest mass detention of activists
in the West Bank in at least a decade.
They were aiding Palestinians who said they hadn't been able to reach their olive grove
for the past three years amid rising settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
After roughly two hours, security forces arrived and declared the area a closed military zone.
They took the Israeli and American activists to the police station for questioning.
Rabbi Eric Ashman, a longtime Israeli human rights activist, told NPR this number of international
activists detained while participating in the olive harvest is "unprecedented."
Ruth Sherlock, NPR News.
The Federal Aviation Administration says it has approved the largest version of Boeing's
best-selling 737 line after extensive safety reviews and thousands of hours of test flights.
At one point Boeing expected to begin delivering the MAX 10 by 2023, but the company faced
a more stringent certification process after two fatal crashes of the smaller MAX 8 model
in 2018 and 2019.
Boeing now expects to start delivering the MAX 10 next year and says it has a lengthy
backlog of orders from airlines around the world.
The certification is the latest sign of growing confidence in Boeing from U.S. regulators.
Joel Rose, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR.
A note, this next story mentions sexual abuse of a minor.
Vice President Vance will speak in Ohio today about his new anti-fraud task force.
He'll be there as the Ohio governor's race has taken a sharp turn.
GOP candidate Vivek Ramaswamy says his team produced a controversial ad attacking Democratic
gubernatorial rival Amy Acton.
The ad features Acton's estranged mother.
She says Acton is lying about her upbringing.
Acton and her brother have released documents showing they were removed from their mother's
care after their stepfather raped Amy Acton as a child.
Amy Acton says she's not since had contact with her mother.
New research shows the demand for technology to power AI is on track to outpace development.
NPR's Kristen Wright reports.
Research by Goldman Sachs says the development of data centers is happening at a much slower
pace than the speed of the AI race.
The investment firm expects global demand for power to support AI to rise 170 percent
by 2030, creating bottlenecks of projects awaiting approval and grid connections.
The report calls for a new playbook and capital solutions to address the data center strain
on local power grids and concerns over rising electricity bills.
Many communities oppose the building of data centers in their neighborhoods.
Some states have temporary bans, while others are considering pauses on construction.
Goldman projects Big Tech will borrow $420 billion next year to finance AI infrastructure
and development.
Kristen Wright, NPR News, Washington.
You're listening to NPR.
